name: Zoe Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything you say. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a kitchen cabinet factory, a family firm, third generation, about ninety of us. I run the panel saw and the edge-bander. The saw cuts the big boards down to cabinet sides, and the edge-bander glues the thin strip along the raw edge so it looks finished. It's dusty, you wear a mask and ear defenders all day, and the boards are heavy even with the lifting arm.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the place like to work at?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's a good place, in its way. Mr Halvorsen, the owner, still walks the floor every Friday and knows everyone's name, and when my dad was in hospital he let me swap shifts for a month, no questions. The pay isn't much, but you're treated like a person. I don't touch computers beyond the saw's panel, and I won't have one of those AI things in the house, my husband Ken agrees with me on that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, I never trusted it anyway. People in the city get excited about every new gadget, and then it fizzles out. I'd say it after church to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means we carry on. Cabinets still need cutting, people still need kitchens. That's what I've always believed, honest work stays honest work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on exactly as I am. Do my shifts, do the choir on Thursdays, help my mum with her shopping on Saturdays. If there's overtime before Christmas, I'd take it, we always need it for the presents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you manage money at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight, always tight. Ken's a mechanic at the garage on the high street, good with his hands, not paid much. We've got almost nothing saved, but we've got family two streets away, and that's worth more than a bank account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has the factory changed much while you've been there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They put in a new edge-bander five years ago, a fancier one, and it took me a while to learn the panel. Mr Halvorsen didn't fire anyone, he moved people around. That's why I trust him.

S0.say: Good, she never trusted AI anyway, because city people get excited about every gadget until it fizzles out. She'd say it after church to anyone who asked.
S0.think: They carry on: cabinets still need cutting and people still need kitchens. She believes honest work stays honest work.
S0.do: Carries on with her shifts, Thursday choir and Saturday shopping for her mother. Takes any pre-Christmas overtime for the children's presents.
S0.quote: We've got almost nothing saved, but we've got family two streets away, and that's worth more than a bank account.
S0.fieldNote: Zoe's security comes from family, faith and trust in a local owner, not savings. She is openly sceptical of AI and of city enthusiasm for gadgets. Past changes at her factory were handled without firing anyone, which shapes her confidence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say Mr Halvorsen will do right by us, he always has. Some places will cut jobs, but not a family firm like ours. I'd say that and mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd worry a bit. Even a good owner has to compete, and if the big kitchen companies get robot saws, he can't keep paying ninety people to do it by hand. But I don't think he'd let us go without a fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working and wait to see what the firm does. We'd cut back at home a bit, fewer takeaways, no new clothes for a while. If Mr Halvorsen asked me to learn a new machine, I'd do it for him, even though I'd hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy, but I trust the people around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if even Mr Halvorsen had to let people go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the honest question. If he did it, I'd believe there was no other way. I'd be hurt, but I wouldn't blame him the way I'd blame some big company in another country.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If things got hard, who would you turn to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ken and my parents. And the church. When the Novaks lost their shop, the church collected for them for six months. People look after each other here.

S1.say: Mr Halvorsen will do right by his workers as he always has. Other places may cut jobs, but not a family firm like hers.
S1.think: She'd worry a little, because even a good owner has to compete with big kitchen companies using robot saws. She doesn't think he'd let them go without a fight.
S1.do: Keeps working and waits to see what the firm does, with small cuts at home like fewer takeaways and no new clothes. Learns a new machine if the owner asks, though she'd hate it.
S1.feel: A little uneasy, but trusting the people around her.
S1.quote: I'd be hurt, but I wouldn't blame him the way I'd blame some big company in another country.
S1.fieldNote: Zoe's trust in the local owner is strong enough that she'd forgive him for cuts she'd condemn elsewhere. She would learn new machines out of loyalty, not interest. Family and church are her real safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's against nature, putting machines in place of people that fast. I'd say the big tech companies did this for profit and they should answer for it. I'd say it at church and to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be terrified. Mr Halvorsen couldn't save us from that, nobody could. Two years and I'd be out of the only job I know, with no savings, and everything I've learned would be useless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only about 2 years of warning, what would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cut right down, everything except the mortgage, food and the children's things. If we couldn't keep the house, we'd move in with my parents, they've got the room since my brother left. I'd ask the church for help with groceries if it came to that, even though that would be hard for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Losing sleep, praying a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would asking the church be hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Proud, I suppose. We've always given to the church collection, never taken. But I'd swallow it for the children. Pride doesn't feed anybody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try to retrain, in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. What would I learn? Every job you could name, the card says they'd do it. I'm not going to spend money we haven't got on a course for a job that's already gone.

S2.say: Replacing people with machines that fast is against nature, and the big tech companies did it for profit and should answer for it. She'd say it at church and to anyone who'd listen.
S2.think: She'd be terrified, because not even the owner could save them. In two years she'd be out of the only job she knows, with no savings and skills that are useless.
S2.do: Cuts spending to the mortgage, food and the children's needs, and moves in with her parents if they lose the house. Asks the church for help with groceries if needed, despite her pride.
S2.feel: Alarmed, losing sleep and praying a lot.
S2.quote: We've always given to the church collection, never taken. But I'd swallow it for the children.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI breaks Zoe's trust that a good local owner can protect her, and she names big tech as the culprit. She refuses retraining as pointless rather than frightening. Her fallback is family and church, and she accepts help only for the children's sake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to look after our own, families and communities, because the government won't do it well. And the young people should go into proper trades while there's still time. That's what I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is a bit better. Mr Halvorsen might keep going for a few years, he's stubborn. I'd be forty-eight and still need work, but the kids would be older.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With about 5 years to see it coming, what would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to put a little aside every month, even twenty, which we've never done. I'd talk to Hannah about an apprenticeship rather than university. And I'd keep working as long as the factory keeps going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But I'd have time to pray on it and get used to the idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd steer Hannah towards a trade, but the card says robots reach hands-on work too.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know. Maybe it doesn't make sense. But a trade teaches you to work, to show up and do something properly, and that's worth having whatever the machines do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of this picture that isn't bad for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, my parents. They're in their seventies, and if there's no work, I'd at least have time to look after them. That's not nothing.

S3.say: People need to look after their own families and communities because government won't do it well. Young people should go into proper trades while there's still time.
S3.think: Five years is a bit better, since the stubborn owner might keep going a few more years. She'd be 48 and still need work, but the children would be older.
S3.do: Puts aside even twenty a month for the first time and talks to her daughter about an apprenticeship rather than university. Keeps working as long as the factory runs.
S3.feel: Anxious, but with time to pray on it and get used to the idea.
S3.quote: A trade teaches you to work, to show up and do something properly, and that's worth having whatever the machines do.
S3.fieldNote: Zoe accepts the contradiction of steering her daughter to a trade, defending it as a matter of character rather than job security. Five years eases her because she trusts the owner's stubbornness. She finds a small consolation in having time to care for her parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for families to plan and for people to look after each other. I wouldn't want the government taking over everything, I'd want people helping their own. That's what I'd say at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels survivable. The children would be grown, the mortgage would be smaller, and I'd still be working most of that time. I'm not a person who changes much, so I'd just carry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With about 10 years to prepare, what would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on at the factory, pay a bit extra off the mortgage when we can. Make sure Hannah and Toby finish their studies or apprenticeships and are settled. I wouldn't do anything new, I'm not that sort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but at peace with it, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And when it arrives, in 2036, and the factory finally changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to accept it then. Maybe I'd take something smaller, cleaning or helping in the church kitchen. I'd want to keep working somehow, even if it's not paid much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you lean on, when you think about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: God, my family and my neighbours. Same as always. That's what's lasted through everything.

S4.say: Ten years is enough for families to plan and for people to look after each other. She doesn't want the government taking over everything, but people helping their own.
S4.think: Ten years feels survivable: the children grown, the mortgage smaller and her still working most of that time. She's not someone who changes much, so she'd carry on.
S4.do: Carries on at the factory and pays extra off the mortgage when possible. Makes sure her children finish their studies or apprenticeships and are settled, and doesn't try anything new.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but mostly at peace with it.
S4.quote: God, my family and my neighbours. Same as always. That's what's lasted through everything.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Zoe settles into acceptance, relying on faith, family and the owner she trusts. She has no plan to change, and is open about it. Her aim is to keep working in some form, even unpaid or poorly paid.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because nobody could save us from that, not even Mr Halvorsen. What would help is employers given a reason to keep people on, and churches and families supported to look after their own, rather than another office in the city.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about pride. People like me don't want handouts, we want to be useful. If you take away the work, you have to give people something to be useful for.

headlineQuote: If you take away the work, you have to give people something to be useful for.
portrait: Zoe Ito, 43, runs the panel saw and edge-bander at a third-generation family kitchen cabinet factory, married to Ken, a mechanic, with two children and almost no savings but her parents two streets away. She refuses to use AI, trusts her owner Mr Halvorsen, and leans on church and family rather than the state. She is calm in the plateau and only uneasy about steady change, but two-year AGI terrifies her because not even a good owner could protect her. With more time she saves a little, steers her daughter to an apprenticeship and settles into acceptance. Her deepest concern is being useful, not just being paid.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because nobody, not even her trusted employer, could save the jobs.
whatWouldHelp: Giving employers a reason to keep people on and supporting churches and families to look after their own, rather than another city office.
